en: Salutations to the illustrious Rīsadāśiva. The first section:
A Compendium of the Essence of the Science of Poisons (Viṣavaidya-sārasamuccaya).
Having tasted the beautiful nectar from the lotus of logic, with a contented heart,
[I praise] that crest-jewel of the twice-born, who dwells within the ocean of the nectar of sacred song,
who delights in the fragrance of the Upanishads, and who is born from the forest of youth.
I constantly revere with devotion my guru, named Śrī Vāsudeva. 1.1.

Having taken refuge at whose lotus feet many have crossed to the further shore of the ocean of scriptures; by a mere fragment of whose compassion impoverished people attained the status of lords of wealth;
and by whose fame this entire world has been made radiant—[salutations] to that [Lord], whose abode is the mountain of Śveta.
I bow to that teacher of ours, the crest-jewel of illustrious Brahmins, a treasure-house of virtues. 1.2.
He who, in ancient times, out of compassion, removed the serpent Kālīya from the Yamunā and purified her whose waters had been corrupted by poison—
that very same one [now delivers] those whose bodies have been swallowed by the serpents of sense-objects within the ocean of worldly existence.
May the Blessed One soon purify us with his side-long glances.
I repeatedly salute Vighneśvara, Vāṇī, Kumāra, and the Lord of Birds, as well as my own gurus, for the removal of obstacles. 1.4
Having examined the treatises on poisons, I shall here compose, in brief, this compendium of their essential points for the benefit of those afflicted by venom.

[The Examination of Inauspicious Days] Having thoroughly examined the defects of the lunar mansions, the day of the week, the lunar date, and so forth, as well as the *viṣṭi* and other inauspicious moments, and the *mṛtyu*, *dagdha*, and other such astrological configurations, the wise man [should proceed]. 1.6.
Having understood the distinction between what is curable and what is incurable, the physician should apply his treatment;
otherwise, that physician will become an object of ridicule in the assembly of people. 1.7
[The Description of the Amṛtakalā] In men, nectar (*amṛta*) is in the right [channel] during the bright fortnight, while elsewhere it is indeed poison (*viṣa*);
for women, it is the reverse, and likewise the reverse occurs during the dark fortnight. (1.8)
[The Description of Difficult Places]: In a garden, on a riverbank, in an empty house, at a crossroads, in a temple, in a cremation ground, on an anthill, or in the hollow of a tree. (1.9)
In the forest, upon a heap of grass, at the edge of a village, in a dilapidated well, at a shrine, at a water-station, in an assembly hall, and in a sacrificial temple. || 1.10 ||
At the roots of the aśvattha and jambū trees, at banyan and udumbara trees, in bamboo thickets, at the junction of roads, at the entrance of a hole, or on a heap of cane, leaves, or stones.
If one bitten by [a snake] on a Śigru, Śleṣmātaka, or Akṣa tree, or likewise on a ruined wall, on a mountain peak, a palace, or an island, does not survive; || 1.12 ||
[The Classification of Vital Points (Marmavibhāga):
Between the two feet, in the belly, at the navel, between the heart and the breasts, on the chest, the shoulders, the throat, the snout, and on the cheeks. 1.13.

From the conch-shell [of the ear], from between the eyebrows, from the crown of the head, from the armpits, from the secret region, from the chin, from the sense organs, from the middle of the arms, and likewise from the top of the head. (1.14)
"If one should be bitten by a snake, no protection exists at all"—thus do those who know the truth declare it to be censurable according to the classification of regions. (1.15)

[The Classification of Messengers] A messenger who carries flowers and other such items in his hands, speaks auspiciously, possesses fortitude, wears clean garments, matches the [king's] complexion and insignia, and is joyful, brings about good fortune. 1.16.

[Auspicious omens: At the time of departure, there is the utterance of auspicious words; the sweet and deep sound of kettledrums, drums, and cymbals; the blast of conch shells; and the sight of a banner, a white flower, milk, curd, clarified butter, and wine.

A Brahmin, a maiden, a king, a cow, a woman of noble family adorned with ornaments, gold, silver, and an elephant— these, when encountered by men as they come toward them, bring about the accomplishment of their undertakings.
[The Messengers of Impurity: One who enters through a non-door, weapon in hand, with eyes fixed on the ground, being negligent;
one with a staff, noose, or similar instrument in hand, exhausted, and speaking with a faltering voice. (1.18)
Clad in a garment of rags from a cemetery, anointed with oil, wearing a black and red flower in his hand, and with his hair loosened, he leaned against dry wood.

One who rubs his breasts, one who clips his nails, one who cuts grass or the like, one who scratches the ground with his feet, one who is physically deformed, a young brahmin student (brahmacārin), one who is distracted, one who weeps, and likewise one who has the smell of a donkey. 1.20.
When such a messenger appears, then misfortune for him is certain.
[Inauspicious omens: One afflicted by disease, with disheveled hair, with trembling feet, wearing black or blood-stained wet garments,
carrying a weapon or a staff, dejected, with a downcast face, and holding a noose in the left hand.

If a widow, a hunchback, one with mangled limbs, a Buddhist mendicant, a follower of Sugata, a wearer of bones, or a matted-hair ascetic should appear before physicians when a person has been bitten [by a snake], they are the bringers of death to that victim. 1.22.
If a messenger, having gone to the west or the left side, should say that there is no poison previously called "the bitten," but there is poison in the opposite case; 1.23.
But if the messenger, having first exhaled toward the right and declared "it is bitten," then goes to the left,
they know that the poison has been neutralized by another.
If one situated on the left first speaks of a serpent and then, moving to the right,
says "he is bewildered," then the person bitten is not alert.
When the two sounds are situated in the same part, they are auspicious;
however, when they are situated in different parts, they indicate the death of the sick person.
When the letters contained in the messenger's speech have been subtracted by the number of the qualities (guṇas),
one should declare that which remains to be accomplished as easy to achieve, difficult to achieve, or impossible to achieve, respectively.
Likewise, having extracted those syllables from the sentence eight times,
[one obtains] a ladle, a circle, a line, a mixture, and even a mouse.
One should consider both the plaything and the falsehood to be poisonless;
yet the messenger stationed in the four directions shall indicate the serpent with its hood.
Likewise, one should indicate a rhinoceros in the corners and a striped snake in their centers;
furthermore, in those subtle regions, one should likewise indicate bulls and other such animals.
Having thus reflected with great subtlety, the wise physician should administer treatment;
likewise, he should observe the messenger stationed in the principal directions and the man who has been bitten.
One should indicate a woman at the corners, or in a transverse breath;
furthermore, if in the beginning of the messenger's speech there should be *kaḥ*, *kiṃ*, *kuḥ*, or *ke*. (1.32)
One should declare that the poison increases slightly in sequence from one, two, three, and four fangs;
and whichever limb the messenger touches, that is the bitten part of the victim.
Remaining motionless, he dwells in happiness; he speaks with ease.
Indeed, among the poisons of moving creatures, they know the venom of the serpent to be the foremost.
Therefore, I shall describe, according to my understanding and in brief, their bite marks, the symptoms of the poison's onset and so forth, as well as their medical treatment. 1.35.
[The description of tooth-bites:
A bite characterized by many mouths with teeth dripping with saliva should be known as *udvamija* (vomited); it is non-venomous for human beings. (1.36)
He whose teeth are dry and receding is to be known as even more formidable than a serpent afflicted by hunger; the same applies to one who has dark spots on his face.
One born from a straight elephant that has been touched is considered more venerable. || 1.38 ||
If it is joined with many slightly reddish spots and accompanied by intoxication, it should be known as the Kālaviṣa [snake] by physicians of keen intellect. (1.39)
That which is endowed with three tusks, broad, filled with flesh,
and joined with blood-filled [temples], is the supreme [form] arising from the enraged Nāga.
Having considered the cause of death and having rejected [other means], one should employ [the ritual] with various severed [limbs] smeared with blood and saliva, provided with flesh. (1.41)
That which is seen caused by gadflies is said to be difficult to cure;
those who know the science of medicine understand it to have arisen from a serpent that has been displaced from its place. (1.42)
[The Description of the Pervasion of the Poison] Having remained for a hundred *mātrās* at the site of the bite, that venom of the victim reaches the forehead, and then the eyes and the face. 1.43.
One should enter the channels and the elements instantly, like oil entering water; the wise call this "the movement from one element to another" (dhātvantaragati). 1.44.
Stiffness of the limbs, heaviness, frequent pain from wind (vāta), lack of self-control, sleepiness,

and horripilation occurring in the body— know that this person has been bitten by a mobile [venomous] creature; in which case there arises the sensation of being mounted [by the insect], along with intense pain from swallowing, swelling, itching, and burning.
In the case of a *daṃśa* sting, this bite is accompanied by a hiss; otherwise, the bite of a *naśaṇa* is indeed devoid of venom.
It produces horripilation when located in the skin; when situated in the blood, it causes perspiration and heat; when residing in the flesh, it brings about discoloration, vomiting, and trembling;
then, reaching the bones, it causes injury to the eyes and throat, or else produces hiccup and labored breathing.
Furthermore, poison located in the marrow causes delusion, while in the semen it brings death to men.
[The Classification of Darvīkara and Others:

The *phaṇin*, *maṇḍalin*, and *rājīla* snakes respectively provoke wind (*vāta*) and the other [humors]; those with mixed characteristics, known as *vyantara*, provoke the combination of all three (*saṃnipāta*). (1.47)
The bite of hooded snakes (phaṇin) is rough, dry, black, and terrifying;
that of the *ghoṇasa* is yellow, hot, accompanied by swelling, and wide.
The bite of those with stripes (rājimat) should be known as cold, oily, excessively swollen, thick with blood, and white in appearance; that of the vyantaras, however, is a mixture of these.
By smelling the fragrance of the ketakī, pāṭalī, mallī, and kaṇavīra flowers,
one should recognize [the presence of] gadflies and the like in due order.
There are four types of bites: those by one, two, or many insects; and the bite itself may be punctured, incised, unbitten, or torn. (1.50)

[The Analysis of the Characteristics of Death] In whose limbs there is perspiration, trembling, and repeated numbness; in whose heart there is labored breathing and a piercing pain, and whose eyes are intensely rolling— || 1.51 ||
One who vomits phlegm and bile, and whose teeth and nails become excessively dark, will certainly fall under the power of death; such is the opinion of the wise.
From the bite-wound of which [insect], O Kṛṣṇa, black blood flows from the bitten one;
there is a blue circular swelling, and the speech becomes nasalized. (1.53)
The passion for looking [at her] is in the armpits, on the palms of the hands, and at the roots of the ears;
the mark of tooth-bites is in the afflicted one's feverish longing. (1.54)
[The examiner: Having reached the vicinity of death, there is indeed no remedy there;
taking up the night, moist with dew and filled with the force of the wind. || 1.55 ||
Having ground the blood from a cock's wound, one should smear it upon the body of the person bitten;
if it becomes hot, the case is curable, but otherwise it is the reverse.
One should not perform any rites there, for they will be fruitless; of this there is no doubt.
If the center of the forehead is pierced with a weapon and no blood is seen, [the person is dead]. (1.57)
Or if it appears slightly black when sprinkled with water, and if there is no bristling of the hair [on its surface] when thrown into water, and if it floats; || 1.58 ||
One upon whose body no scar from the stroke of a staff is visible should be known as one whose life has been liberated; there is no need for further deliberation on this matter.
One whose bite is life-threatening should be submerged in a reservoir of water;
if many bubbles are immediately seen [rising], he is dead.
If the physician does not remain attentive for half a nāḍī, then only one [pulse] is seen there; likewise, after a slight delay of time.
Having observed the appearance of a bubble and having quickly extracted it, the physician should carefully protect the eye with dry nasal medications and collyriums. 1.62.
Having thus correctly examined one afflicted by poison from the perspective of the treatises,
a wise person should quickly treat the curable case and reject the other.
[The symptoms of the onset of hooded-snake venom and its treatment:
In the first stage of the onset of hooded snakes (*phaṇin*), there occurs intense burning at the site of the bite;
in that case, the physician should perform bloodletting by means of venesection and other such methods. (1.64)
In the second stage, the body becomes dark-brown and knots (nodules) arise;
having pierced a vein there, one should drink black pepper with ghee.
In the third-day fever (tṛtīyaka), there is piercing pain, dependence on others, and sleepiness;
in that case, one should first drink cold water mixed with uśīra and sandalwood.

If the poison is in the fourth house, there will be a piercing pain in the limbs accompanied by contraction; there will also be an obstruction of feces and urine, and in such a case, the physician should administer a purgative.
Having ground *taṇḍulīya* and *aśvagandhā* with water, one should administer it;
it will cause the poison to reach the fifth stage, resulting in deafness and pain in the heart.
In the case of swelling of the breast, the wise physician should pierce a vein in the middle and administer potassium carbonate (ṭaṅkaṇa) for the infant to drink.
In the sixth month, the child may suffer from heart disease, labored breathing, hiccups, fainting, and other such ailments.
One should administer dry nasal drops or collyrium with the juice of *bhṛṅgarāja*;
otherwise, on the seventh day, there would be loss of life, so the best of physicians should act accordingly.
[General Treatment for Darvīkara Snakes: Having properly administered nasal drops, collyrium, and other remedies, one should protect the life-force (*prāṇa*).
Then, having ground *vacā*, asafoetida (*hiṅgu*), and *uṣaṇa* in the fresh juice of *kiṃśuka*, [one should apply it]. (1.71)
This supreme medicine, having been processed individually with the milks of *tilvaka*, *arka*, and *snuhī*, destroys the poison of all ladles (venoms) through application as an ointment.
For seven days, borax is supremely beneficial for those bitten by snakes; this has been kept secret by the wise in the form of drinks, nasal drops, and ointments.
Garlic, asafoetida, and the three pungents (savyoṣa), processed with the milk of the *arka* plant,
destroy all types of *darvī* poison in an instant when administered as nasal drops, by drinking, or other means.

Having ground together *unmattapatra*, *sindhūttha* (rock salt), and betel leaf, an errhine (*nasya*) prepared with the liquid resulting from that paste is beneficial for *darvīviṣa* (venom of the *darvī* class).
Black pepper, having been repeatedly saturated with the fresh juice of *śirīṣa* flowers and dried, should be used to prepare collyrium and other such preparations with that very same juice.
Having ground *arka* leaves with salt in sandalwood water, one shall destroy all *darvī* poisons by means of an ointment; of this there is no doubt. (1.77)

Thus has the treatment for the venom of the *darvīkara* snake been briefly stated by the physician who has conquered [his foes]. Now, the treatment for those bitten by the *maṇḍalin* snake is described by me here.
[The characteristics of the poison of a circular-marked snake and its treatment:
When the circular-marked snake's poison is located in the skin, the skin becomes yellowish and there is a burning sensation.
In that case, one should sprinkle it with cold water and drink sandalwood mixed with water. (1.79)
In the second stage, trembling and paleness arise in the body;
having first drained the blood from that area, one should apply ushira and sandalwood paste.
And one should have this drunk with water; it removes the poison of snakes.
In the third [type of] poison, that of the *maṇḍalin* snakes, sleep and thirst arise.
An application of Madhuka and Uśīra, cooled, destroys poison.
In the fourth stage, the fevered patient indeed suffers from muteness, piercing pain, and swelling.
In that case, the physician should have the patient drink triphalā with cold water;
[the symptoms include] obstruction in the bones and eyes, burning sensation, and likewise mental confusion. (1.83)
In that case, having first released the blood, one should cause him to drink sandalwood mixed in water.
Furthermore, in the sixth stage, there is a general sinking of the limbs and obstruction of the nose.
One should grind the root of punarnavā and have it drunk with lukewarm water;
[otherwise], there will be a paralysis of all the sense organs, or death in the case of white [leprosy].
In that case, the best of physicians should administer dry treatments such as nasal drops (nasya) and collyrium (añjana). [General treatment for maṇḍalī:
With madder (māñjiṣṭhā), lodhra, bilva, arka, the two types of turmeric (rajanī), and sandalwood (candana)... 1.86.
One should prepare a drink, an ointment, and so forth from equal parts of the roots of śirīṣa and pāṭalī and sarala; this destroys the poison of the maṇḍalī spider.
Having ground the roots of *varṣābhū*, *snuhī*, and *dineśa*, one should apply it with cow’s urine to the bite; this destroys the poison of *maṇḍalī* and *ikṣveḍa* snakes.
Having ground yaṣṭī, vacā, candana, uśīra, rāsnā, and bhallātaka with milk, one should administer it by drinking and other means; this destroys the poison of the maṇḍalī snake. 1.89.
Fresh butter, curd, honey, combined with rock salt and the three pungents (vyoṣa),
destroys the poison of the *ghoṇasa* snake and the cobra in an instant through drinking, external application, and other means.
Having ground neem bark and the root of *nīlikā* with the juice of *nīlī*, one who has been bitten by a red-spotted spider should consume it for the sake of pacifying the poison. (1.91)
[The treatment for complications caused by poison:
One should cook the fruit of *dhurdhūra* together with an equal amount of rock salt (*saindhava*) in sour gruel (*āranāla*).
Then, having ground it, one should apply it as a paste; this is an excellent remedy for removing swelling. 1.92.
Having ground together the leaves of the *unmatta* plant and *tintriṇī*, along with the dung of a buffalo, one should apply it as a plaster; this destroys the poison of the *maṇḍalī* snake.
One should sprinkle the ulcer with lukewarm ghee mixed with rock salt;
this is the supreme secret taught by the wise for the destruction of swelling, heat, and pricking pain. 1.94.
If the urine becomes yellowish in color due to the poison of a *maṇḍalī* snake,
one should grind the bark of *naktamāla* and administer it with lukewarm water.
If one bitten by [a venomous creature] is afflicted by heat, then sandalwood should be used;
whether it is drunk or applied as an ointment, the poison will be instantly neutralized. (1.96)
One afflicted by thirst from being bitten by a *maṇḍalī* snake should drink the juice of the *rambhā* root with water;
if there is pain in the head, one should take the root of *kākatiktaka* mixed with milk.
Having ground [these] with milk, one who drinks it will immediately find relief from headache.
Likewise, having boiled *āmalakī*, *carma*, milk, and *mustā* in equal parts, [one should drink it]. 1.98.
Having ground sandalwood mixed with [the poison], one should apply it as a forehead-mark (lalāṭikā).
If the bitten person vomits blood, he should drink milk with neem leaves.
Likewise, one should grind the root of the *āraṇyapāṭalī* and have it drunk;
or, if the person afflicted by fever has been bitten, [one should give] the bark of the root of the *tintriṇī*.
Having ground [the plant] in milk, one should drink it; the person bitten is immediately freed from fever.
If flatulence arises in one bitten by a snake, then the physician [should act]. 1.101.
One should cause [the patient] to drink rock salt (*sindhūttha*), *abhayā*, and *viśva* with lukewarm water;
if there is obstruction of urine (*mūtrarodha*), then [one should give] cardamom (*elā*) together with *kaṇā*.
Having ground it, one should drink it with lukewarm water or else with coconut water;
one should also apply a stream from a golden vessel to the navel for the sake of pacifying its obstruction. (1.103)
In cases of hiccup, one should lick a powder of the three pungents (vyoṣa) and raisins combined with the juice of citron (bījapūra),
or alternatively, the powder of vālaka mixed with honey.
In cases of bladder pain,
abdominal distension, and constipation, one should prepare a medicinal suppository (phalavarti) consisting of sāragvadha, trivṛt, upakulyā, and harītakī.
One should drink [this mixture] with ghee and honey, which destroys pain in the bladder and other ailments;
it consists of equal parts of bhūnimba, kaṭukā, trāyantī, and indrayava.
One should drink two parts of *citraka* and eight parts of *kuṭaja* with water;
this removes poison, dysentery, upward movement of wind (*udāvarta*), cough, asthma, and fever. (1.107)
In cases of bloody diarrhea, one should eat the bark or the inner skin of the *kuṭaja* root, well-ground with lukewarm water; by this, the disease of diarrhea is instantly destroyed. (1.108)
Trivṛt, processed for three days with a decoction of triphalā and stirred with ghee, when drunk, destroys swelling caused by poison. (1.109)
[The treatment for disorders of wind caused by poison:
One should drink castor oil mixed with goat meat broth; or, while consuming the broth of fatty meat, one may drink ghee and oil together at once. 1.110
One should cause [the patient] to drink cotton-root, black pepper, the two types of turmeric, nalada, nala, long pepper, svārjikā, and kuṣṭha, having stirred them together with water.
For a person who is insane from the wind of poison or likewise afflicted by epilepsy,
the general procedure alone is sufficient for the pacification of all complications.
A specific rule is stated here for the swift pacification of disease:
[the symptoms of the stages of *rājila* venom and their treatment].
When bitten by one whose venom resides in the skin (*tvac*), the victim becomes white-bodied. (1.113)
Immediately after the blood has been released, one should drink ginger with lukewarm water;
on the second day, sliminess at the site of the bite and reddish skin appear. (1.114)
The physician should cauterize the bite there with iron heated by fire;
afterwards, he should have the patient drink guḍūcī with pungent spices and lukewarm water.

In the case of the third type of fever, or when the poison originates from the *rājila* snake, there will be heat and a flow of water from the mouth and eyes; in that situation, [one should apply] salt (*saindhava*).
In the fourth stage, one should lick trikaṭu with honey;
if there is obstruction of speech, swelling, piercing pain, fever, and vomiting, one should treat them as previously described.
When the ringed-snake venom resides in the bones, phlegm increases excessively;
it then suddenly causes hiccup and contraction of the throat.
Having expelled the blood, one should drink Sindhu-stone (saindhava) salt with the three pungents (vyoṣa) mixed with honey.
When the poison of a Rājila snake has reached the marrow, it causes pain in the heart, cough, and suppression of breath.
Fainting occurs there; by adding salt and garlic to the juice of *kāravallī* and administering it, one may overcome that poison with difficulty.

If death itself should occur on the seventh [day], one should write that [mantra] upon the crown of the head and apply a proven medicinal drug; one should also perform dry nasal therapy, collyrium, and other such treatments.

[General Treatment for *Rājila* Snakes]: Having stirred together cow dung water with honey, rock salt (*saindhava*), and *māgadhī*, one should administer it; one should also give *śāribā* root as a drink and prepare a nasal medication (*nasya*) with auspicious water (*śivāmbu*). (1.122)
One should cause [the patient] to drink the root of *āraṇyakāravallī* with milk, or a paste of *vyoṣa* mixed with the fresh juice of the leaves of *vahninirguṇḍikā*. (1.123)
In all cases of the poison of *rājila* snakes, one should administer nasal therapy (*nasya*) according to the specific condition,
using *kimpāka*, *aśvagandhā*, and the root of *nīlī*.
For the poison of the *rājīmat* plants, one should grind [the remedy] with *āranāla* and drink it;
for the poison of the *saṅkara* plants, one should employ everything previously mentioned.

According to the specific dosha, according to the symptoms, and according to the stage of the disease, the best of physicians [in the treatment of vomiting] should administer a powder prepared from black pepper, añjana, vaidehī, and red ochre (gairika). 1.126.
Combined with the juice of the citron (bījapūraka), it destroys vomiting.

For the benefit of the world, I shall here concisely describe the symptoms of the onset and the characteristics of the poison of all snakes, such as the hooded cobras and others, who are afflicted by venom, along with the remedies for them.
I have spoken here; may the wise purify it out of compassion.
Thus ends the first part.
Now begins the second part.
Furthermore, I shall describe, according to my understanding and in brief, the characteristics of the poisons of rats, scorpions, spiders, and so forth, as well as their medical treatment.
[The Treatment of Rat Poison] Furthermore, rats here discharge their poison in five ways: by means of white excrement, urine, nails, teeth, or [saliva]. (2.2)
General symptoms include the arising of knots, swellings, caruncles, and circular patches; as well as severe thickening of the calves, erysipelas, and kiṭibha eruptions. (2.3)
There is splitting pain in the joints, intense agony, fainting, prostration of the limbs, fever, weakness, loss of appetite, dyspnea, vomiting, and horripilation. (2.4)
When the *mauṣika* disorder is located in the skin, pricking and itching arise;
one should then extract the blood from the milk [of the animal] and administer the five parts of the *śirīṣa* tree.
When the blood is affected, knots and burning sensations arise; at that time, the physician, having let out the blood, should have the patient drink *taṇḍulīyaka* with milk. (2.6)
In the third stage, there is yellow urine, headache, and fever;
one should administer the root of *aṅkola* with milk or else with sour gruel (*kāñcika*). 2.7.
When swellings and circular eruptions arise due to the vitiation of the fat and the joints,
one should then have the patient drink a decoction of *makkuṇa* with the fresh juice of the *śirīṣa* leaf.
If the fifth house contains the sign of Taurus, vomiting, burning sensations, and pain arise;
in that case, one should administer all treatments such as nasal drops using oil. (2.9)

When that poison has reached the marrow, fainting and burning sensations occur; at that time, the physician should employ the juice of the five parts of the *śirīṣa* tree for nasal administration and other treatments.
If the poison is located in the seventh house, death will inevitably occur for men;
one should quickly perform its protection by means of proven nasal drops, collyrium, and other such remedies.

[The general treatment for rat poison: One should administer it as a drink or apply it as an ointment, using well-ground mustā, salt, varṣābhū, and the roots of nīlī, mixed either with milk or the juice of kanyā. (2.12)
The root of the *arka* plant, together with the five parts of the *śirīṣa*, combined with *māleya* and soaked in honey,
when drunk with milk, destroys [the effects of] rat poison.
Just as the sun [destroys] poison that is most terrible, so does he [destroy] darkness. || 2.13 ||
[A decoction of *nīlī*, *karañja*, and so forth, for the purpose of neutralizing rat poison:
*nīlī*, *karañja*, *picumanda*, *śirīṣa*, *śigru*, *mustā*, *ugrā*, *viśva*, *surabhuruha*, and *candana*.
This water, when combined with these [substances] in equal proportions and fully matured, quickly destroys the entire web of defects arising from mice. (2.14)
Then, the physician should powder equal amounts of *bṛhatī* root and *triphalā*, grind them together with the milk of *snuhī*, and form them into pills. (2.15)
Having placed them in a crystal vessel, one should dry them again in the sun;
then, each one mixed with ghee and combined with food, one should eat it in the morning. (2.16)
This secret remedy, prepared with the fresh juice of *trāyantī* and combined with *śaṅkhapuṣpī* and *varā*, destroys the poison of all rats; it has been preserved by the wise. (2.17)
Ghee, when administered through drinking and other means, destroys the entire poison of a rat in an instant;
likewise, [ghee] with the paste of the five parts [of the śirīṣa tree] processed in the juice of the śirīṣa leaves [achieves the same]. (2.18)
Matured oil, prepared with the juice of *śaṅkhapuṣpī* and mixed with a paste of *yaṣṭīmadhuka*, quickly destroys the accumulation of morbid humors caused by mice. (2.19)
Oil with ten times its weight of milk is the supreme antidote for the poison of rats;
furthermore, having ground cotton sprouts and stirred them again with milk, [one should apply it].
Having submerged up to his neck in water, having drunk and discarded the vessel, he should then perform an immersion once more in the water behind him. (2.21)
[The characteristics of scorpion venom and its treatment:
Thus, this should be performed for three days to pacify the poison of rats. Hereafter follow the stages and symptoms of poisons arising from scorpions. (2.22)
And I shall describe its treatment for the benefit of embodied beings:
he who experiences incessant trembling, vomiting, confusion, pain, exhaustion, perspiration, and a burning sensation, as well as horripilation;
Moreover, they know that when this man's blood at the site of the bite becomes excessively agitated by thirst, he is as if bitten by a scorpion. || 2.23 ||
When the scorpion venom resides in the skin, there is frequent pricking pain;
when it resides in the blood, there is burning in the limbs, hiccup, and knots in the third stage.
In the fourth [day] there is dryness of the throat and a violent fever; then in the fifth, mental distress;
in the sixth, a burning of the mind; and in the seventh, redness of the eyes.
If death should occur there, one must perform the remedy quickly;
in the case of being bitten by a scorpion or by a creature with potent venom, one should extract the blood using horns or similar means.
For the supreme pacification of suffering, this alone must be performed by a physician who is well-informed.
One should perform nasal drops with a paste of *aśvagandhā* ground with the juice of *arka* leaves;
and one should apply an ointment made from black *nimba* combined with black pepper. (2.27)
One should administer a continuous stream (dhārā) of these two combined with buttermilk (takra),
or here, nasal drops (nāvana) consisting of the juice of *tintriṇī* mixed with rock salt (*saindhava*).
One afflicted by poison should apply collyrium to the eyes with this very [substance];
having thoroughly rubbed a karañja sprout with both hands, [one should use it]. (2.29)
Applied to a bite, it effortlessly destroys the poison arising from a scorpion;
furthermore, asafoetida that has been heated should be placed in a bronze vessel. (2.30)
Then, having rubbed it with the juice of betel leaves, one should apply it to the sting;
the affliction caused by a scorpion will quickly perish, without a doubt. (2.31)
Incense made from peacock feathers, cock feathers, rock salt, and sesame seeds is a swift destroyer of the poisons arising from scorpions. (2.32)
Incense made from nimba leaves, human hair, turmeric, vajra, tāla leaves, and grain husks, combined with a feather smeared with ghee, shall destroy the venom arising from a scorpion sting. (2.33)

[The Treatment of Spider Poison] Spiders discharge poison in seven ways: through saliva, claws, urine, fangs, dust, feces, and their genital organ; this poison is endowed with fierce, middling, or weak potency. (2.34)
[The general characteristics of spider venom:
In the case of spider venom, there will be pustules at the site of the bite, swelling and eruptions all around, blackish discoloration, pricking pain, headache, and fever. (2.35)
In the first stage of a spider's bite, itching and blackness arise;
having let out the blood, one should apply an ointment of *tulasī* and turmeric.
And likewise, one should cause [the patient] to drink [the medicine]; thereafter, trembling and horripilation arise intensely at first; in that case, one should drink *tulasī* with milk. (2.37)
In the third stage, eruptions, swelling, and thirst arise;
the drinking and external application of sandalwood, ushira, and madhuka are recommended. (2.38)
In the fourth stage, during the onset of *lūtikā*, as well as in fever and eruptions, circular patches (*maṇḍala*) may appear; the roots of indigo and *śirīṣa* [should be used]. (2.39)
Having ground that very [substance] with its own juice, it is beneficial for drinking, as an ointment, and so forth.
When [the moon] is in the fifth house, emaciation of the body and the tongue arises. (2.40)
In that case, one should administer the root of *taṇḍulīyaka* with milk.
When [Mars] is situated in the sixth house, it causes pain in the palate and head, as well as fever and delusion. (2.41)
One should drink sandalwood with milk along with fragrant ushira and nili;
when the seventh defect of the lūtikā has departed, thirst arises. (2.42)
If fainting and delusion should occur there, one should diligently administer nasal drops, potions, and other treatments with lice-killing herbs according to the prescribed rule. (2.43)
[General Treatment for Spider Poison] One should grind the five parts of the *śirīṣa* tree and have the patient drink it with milk in the morning;
one should also apply a plaster of *naktamāla* with water, which removes that poison. (2.44)
Tagara, garlic, the three pungents (vyoṣa), kuṣṭha, madhuka, and sandalwood, well-prepared with the fresh juice of nirguṇḍī, tulasī, and nīlī; 2.45.
Gopāṅganā, aśvagandhā, and rajanī also [neutralize] the force of poison; oil well-ground with these [substances] destroys the venom of spiders. 2.46.
A decoction well-prepared with these is the supreme destroyer of spider venom:
[a decoction] of nirguṇḍī, śārivā, uśīra, kuṣṭha, ambu, nata, and candana. (2.47)
A decoction made from the roots of *nīlikā* and *pāṭalī*, along with *surasā* and *pāṭhā*, removes the pain caused by spiders when administered during the onset of their poison.
This [remedy], which has been observed by us to yield immediate results, is combined with *vireka* and *trivṛt*;
it includes *lodhra*, *sevya*, *patmaka*, the pollen of *patmara*, that which is called *kālīya*, and red sandalwood.
The flower of the *kāntā* plant, the milk of the *dugdhinī*, lotus stalks,
and all types of spiders destroy [the fetus] by means of every possible action.
In this decoction of *nīlikālī* boiled with husks, one should add garlic, horse-fragrance (*aśvagandhā*), and well-ground pastes of *trikaṭu*,
*rajanī*, *kuṣṭha*, *uśīra*, and *gandhā*.
Let him cook and drink ghee for the sake of pacifying the pain caused by the spider.

Success is achieved by boiling garlic, *tulasī*, *kākamācī*, and *aśvagandhā* in water with indigo, along with the pastes (*kalka*) of the three pungents (*trikaṭu*), turmeric, sandalwood, and vetiver;
or even in a decoction (*kaṣāya*) prepared from the roots of *tulasī*.
Clarified butter removes all poison arising from spiders as well as erysipelas.
[The Treatment of the Alarka Venom] For one bitten by a dog, black blood flows from the wound;
there may be swelling, piercing pain, fever, and fear of public assemblies. (2.52)
One should cauterize the bite with cooked ghee mixed with rock salt;
or, having ground the root of *vāṅkola* with sour gruel (*āranāla*), one should apply it as a paste.
One should employ *aṅkola* in the cooking of oils, fats, and clarified butter everywhere;
it is the supreme medicine against the poisons of dogs. (2.54)
[The Efficacious Medicine: Garlic and the root of *vyāghrapād* shall each be half a part;
having ground them together with the juice of *aṅkola* bark, one should [apply it]. 2.55.
Or one may practice this for three days with milk or *āranāla*;
thus, a mortal who eats wholesome food is completely freed from the poison of a dog. (2.56)
On the fourth day, the patient should follow a wholesome diet as before;
a decoction made from the roots of *nīlī* and *karañja* destroys the poison of dogs. (2.57)
[The decoction of nīlī, karañja, and others: with nīlī, karañja, tulasī, picumanda, lodhra, dārvī, yava, the two types of bṛhatī, parpaṭa, and abda;
Milk boiled with equal parts of vyoṣa, śirīṣa, and suradāru should be administered to ward off the delusions caused by poison.
Powdered *guḍūcī* essence combined with the three pungents (*kaṭutraya*), taken together with sugar and clarified butter, destroys the poison of dogs. (2.59)

[The specific treatment for the venom of the *alarka* spider: Having ground the seed of the *unmatta* plant, it should be drunk with the water from its leaves; this is the supreme medicine against the poisons of dogs and jackals.
Having drunk it in the morning, the physician should then, at the end of three watches,
thoroughly sprinkle the head of the bitten person with cold water.
The patient should then follow a wholesome diet for three days, as previously prescribed.
[Characteristics and Treatment of Nakula-poisoning:
The palate, lips, and teeth become black, the eyes are red, and there is fever. (2.61)
When poison originates from a mongoose, there is a contraction of the neck and suppression of speech;
[this is countered] by Nirguṇḍī, Kanyā, and Bhṛṅga, well-blended with their own expressed juices.
This poison is destroyed in an instant by [the application of] black, smeared, or yellow [substances].
[The symptoms and treatment for cat-poisoning:
There is itching at the site of the bite, eruptions, and a bluish discoloration at the palate and the navel. (2.63)
In the case of poison derived from a cat, there may be fever and piercing pain accompanied by vomiting;
one should cause the person to drink *pathyā* mixed with alkali and *citrā*, along with honey.
One should apply trikaṭu and rock salt here, combined with the juice of bhṛṅga;
having applied asafoetida in the juice of bhṛṅga and drunk it, one shall conquer poison.
[The characteristics of the horse-poison and its treatment:
When there is constant swelling at the site of the bite as well as the flow of blood, and the eyes then become nearly closed and filled with tears— 2.66.
One should know that the horse has been bitten by that [creature]; there, one should administer medical treatment:
having ground vacā, lodhra, and aśvagandhā with milk, one should have it drunk.
[The characteristics of the monkey-poison and its treatment: If the bite is black, there is excessive bleeding, suppuration, sloughing, and horripilation;
And if the teeth, lips, and skin become dark, one should know that this person has been bitten by a species of monkey.
Having ground the five parts of the *śirīṣa* tree with milk, one should drink it and also apply it as an ointment;
thus, the poison originating from a monkey shall be pacified.
[The characteristics of a poisonous person and their treatment:
He who suffers from muteness, piercing pain in the limbs, and excessive fever;
whose teeth and lips are darkened, and from whose mouth saliva flows— || 2.69 ||
If redness appears in both eyes, one should know that the person is afflicted by human poison;
having ground *taṇḍulīya*, *vacā*, and *nīlī*, one should have it drunk with milk.
If a mortal applies [this remedy], he is released from the poison born of human teeth.
[The characteristics of frog-poison and its treatment:
Pustules accompanied by swelling appear at the site of the bite.
Itching, severe fever, thirst, vertigo, and so forth, as well as flatulence— if these occur in a person, they know him to be bitten by a *durdura* snake. (2.71)
[The characteristics of poison from a Brahmin woman and its treatment: In this regard, by grinding the three pungents (tryūṣaṇa) together with asafoetida (rāmaṭha),
one may remove the venom of a *maṇḍūka* through drinking milk, external applications, and other such means.
Poison arising from the bite of a *brāhmaṇī* snake is generally like that of a [common] snake;
for its pacification, a decoction of the root of *nīlī* should be drunk here. (2.72)
Having ground the bark of *śigru*, *nimba*, *karañja*, *dīrghavṛnta*, and *śirīṣa*, it should be drunk for the pacification of *brāhmaṇī* poison. (2.73)
This same procedure is also recommended for the venom of a lizard (*kṛkalāsa*).
[The characteristics of centipede venom and its treatment:
The venom produced by a centipede bite is of two kinds: that which is [directly] from its body-fluid and that which is from its saliva. (2.74)

For the pacification of a bite, one should grind the five parts of the *śirīṣa* tree together with the three pungent spices (*kaṭutraya*) and apply them as an ointment or employ them in other ways. 2.75.
In the case of a specific vitiation by rasa, eruptions (koṭha) appear; there is discoloration and itching of the skin. The medical treatment for that is as follows: || 2.76 ||
One should apply *bhūnimba* and *ketakī* leaves fried in coconut oil for the sake of its pacification, and one should also employ indigo oil. || 2.77 ||
A decoction (kaṣāya) prepared with the group of drugs beginning with āragvadha is also highly beneficial.
[The drugs in this group are: āragvadha, indrayava, pāṭalī, kākatiktā, nimba, amṛtā, madhurasā, sruvavṛkṣa, and pāṭhā.
Bhūnimba, sairyaka, paṭola, the two types of karañja, saptacchada, agni, suṣavī, the fruit of bāṇa, and ghoṇṭā.
The group beginning with Āragvadha conquers vomiting, skin diseases, poisons, and fevers;
it subdues phlegm, itching, and urinary disorders, and acts as a purifier of malignant ulcers.
[The characteristics of scorpion venom and its treatment:
Equal parts of *naktamāla*, the two types of *niśā*, *bhūtīka*, and the seeds of *arka* [should be used]. (2.78)

For the destruction of the *gaulikā* poison, one should apply a plaster made of the three pungent spices (*savyoṣa*) ground together with a handful (*añjalikara*) of fresh butter. [The characteristics of the fly-poison and its treatment. 2.79 (1)
One should apply an ointment for the pacification of the poison of a fly.
[Regarding the characteristics of betel-nut and snake poisons, and their treatment:
one should drink the fresh juice of the leaves of the *Ikṣvāku* plant.
It destroys the poison of the *tāmbūlanāga* snake;
or else, one afflicted by poison should immediately drink asafoetida (*hiṅgu*) dissolved in water from the hollow of a cloud. 2.79 (2)
[The characteristics of *gara* poison and its treatment:

When *gara* poison is located in the stomach of a mortal, many complications arise; however, when the *gara* poison is located in the large intestine (*pakvāśaya*), one should purify it by means of emetics and purgatives. 2.80.
When that [poison] is located in the stomach (āmāśaya), the physician should cause the patient to vomit. [Examination for determining the location of the poison:
Having taken indigo leaves and ground them, one should apply [the paste] with milk. (2.81)
Where the belly of a sick person does not dry up even after a long time, one should know that poison resides there; so say those who are experts in poisons. 2.82.
Furthermore, for one whose purification has been performed, in order to exhaust the remainder of the defects,
one should grind the root of white *pārantī* with milk and have him drink it.
Accompanied by mantras according to the scriptures, or else called *pṛthuka*, along with *rudrākṣa* beads, gold, and *vacā* root, [it counteracts] the onset of poison. (2.84)
Thus has been briefly explained the medical treatment for the administration of poison.
[The characteristics of stationary poisons and their treatment: Now, the characteristics of poisons produced from stationary sources (sthāvara) [are described]. 2.85.
I shall now explain its medical treatment briefly, according to my understanding,
by means of leaves, flowers, fruits, bark, resins, milky sap, and seeds.
Poison originating from stationary sources arises from the juices of bulbous roots and similar parts;
it causes the patient to speak many words, produces heat, exhaustion, and fever, and brings about vomiting and the obstruction of phlegm, feces, and urine.
Thus, where these various terrible transformations are seen, they recognize here that man as afflicted by poisons arising from stationary beings. (2.87)
Having ground together the root of nīlī, rock salt (saindhava), taṇḍulīya, and fermenting agent (kiṇva), one should apply it as a drink, an ointment, or for other uses;
or one may drink this same mixture with milk, omitting the rock salt.
That poison arising from a stationary source would perish instantly.
In this case, having ground the root of the indigo plant in its own leaf-water,
it shall immediately destroy any poison— whether stationary or mobile— by drinking it, by applying it as an ointment, or by sprinkling it.
But this fault has been stated by all the learned. (2.89)
Fresh butter derived from *bhallātaka* quickly destroys poison;
in this case, an application with clarified butter washed a hundred times is the supreme remedy. (2.90)
[The symptoms of poison in animals and their treatment:
At the site of the bite, there is swelling, horripilation, fever,
trembling of the head, and lack of clarity in the eyes.
If the flow of saliva from cows is frothy,
one should know that this poison has originated from a mobile source.
At the time of its excessive growth, one should perform excision, cauterization, or scarification;
[one should apply] a stream of ghee mixed with rock salt.
One should immediately apply [this] here for the pacification of poison. || 2.92 ||
Poison originating from moving creatures [such as snakes] is destroyed by a *khārī* measure of equal parts of *vacā*, *nāgara*, *sindhūttha*, *pippalī*, and *marica*, ground together. 2.93.
The root of nīlī, the two types of niśā,
combined with taṇḍulīyaka and also joined with the five parts of śirīṣa, should be ground together in a large mortar.
Poison is destroyed by means of drinks and other such remedies; this is supremely beneficial for animals.
Likewise, salt and garlic [are used] in a juice made from the sprouts and leaves of the *mañjarī* plant.
This drink, consisting of *śirīṣa*, vermilion, garlic, *vacā*, and black pepper, immediately destroys poison in quadrupeds and is likewise effective for humans.
By grinding it in fermented rice-water (āranāla) and administering it as a drink and so forth, one destroys the poison of cows in an instant.
Sataṇḍulīyaka and śarapuṅkhapatra, combined with the juice of girikarṇikā and accompanied by abhiṣava, immediately destroy the poison of animals when drunk. (2.98)
Those who are afflicted by poison, those who eat unwholesome food, and those who eat wholesome food.
Oil, black gram, horse gram, molasses, salt, liquor, fish, meat, and sour substances;
buttermilk, curd, daytime sleep, or conversely, staying awake at night, sexual indulgence;
smoke, fire, sunlight, exposure to wind, and the consumption of tobacco leaves and the like.
"Those who understand the meaning of the medical treatises have declared that these must be avoided incessantly by those afflicted by poison. (3.1)

For those afflicted by poison, rice known as *ṣaṣṭika* is wholesome when eaten and possesses many virtues; likewise, the various types of *kūṣmāṇḍa* fruit and vegetables such as *taṇḍulīya* are highly beneficial.
Cow’s milk that is not curdled is salutary here, as is any food that is sweet, unctuous, and light.
Having investigated correctly through reasoning, one should [understand] everything, such as the humors (doṣas) and the affected tissues (dūṣyas), by way of the course of the poison. 3.2.
Having placed the leaves of *musalī*, *lāṅgalī*, *nimba*, *śirīṣa*, and *bakula* into a large earthen vessel (*khārī*) and boiled them, one should administer a fomentation (*sveda*). 3.3.

Some consider the steaming of grains to be beneficial; among them, the *priyaṅgu* seeds are said by those skilled in the art of steaming to be the best. One should employ everything prescribed for this in the ritual bathing as well. (3.4)
Oil prepared with indigo water and strained through a cloth soaked in its roots is an excellent remedy for one afflicted by poison, whether used for bathing, massage, or other such applications.
Water mixed with one part each of *niśā*, *garala*, and *vṛkṣākṣa*, and three, four, and five parts [of other ingredients],
should be boiled down until only one-fourth remains.
One should employ it for bathing, as it is supremely beneficial for those afflicted by poison;
having boiled the fruit of the *dhātrī* in milk and ground it, one should apply it to the head. (3.7)
One should smear the root of *nīlī* together with camphor upon the head; likewise, an application of both *devadālī* and *niśā* on the crown of the head removes poison. (3.8)
Having ground pāṭhā, the root of śirīṣa, house-soot, and rock salt together with bhṛṅga-water, an application on the head removes poison. (3.9)
Having ground sandalwood, uśīra, rock salt, the three pungents (kaṭutraya),
and [other ingredients] in the juice of bhṛṅgarāja, an application on the head destroys the force of poison.
An incense made from equal parts of tiger skin,
musk, bone, and mongoose hair, powdered and anointed with sheep’s milk, removes all poisons.

[General Treatment for Snakebites] If the specific species of snake is not known here due to the previously mentioned characteristics, and the physician is told that the onset of poison has occurred: 3.12.
This is the general medical treatment for the protection of those afflicted by poison. [Treatment for Immediate Bites:
One who has just been bitten should immediately bite that very snake-eater (the mongoose). 3.13.
Having broken a stick, a clod of earth, or similar objects with his teeth, he then acted with great agitation.
One should smear the bite with spittle or earwax;
one should bind an *ariṣṭā* plant four finger-breadths above the bite. (3.15) [The Binding of the *Ariṣṭā*]
By means of linen and other cloths, by braided hair, by perfected mantras, and by the binding of one who knows the mantras, poison is checked like water by the construction of a dam. (3.16)
The veins of such a person do not carry the poison when they are constricted by a ligature;
therefore, one should extract the bite after squeezing it out, provided it is not located in a vital organ (marman) or at a joint.
The force of the poison does not arise, just as a sprout does not emerge from the destruction of its seed;
or one may cauterize the bite—excluding that of a *maṇḍalin* snake—with gold, iron, and so forth.
Fire reduces a mass of poison to ashes in an instant.
Especially that which is fleshy and located within the shadow of the arishta. || 3.19 ||
One should repeatedly smear the limb, along with the insect bite itself, with medicinal ointments,
and sprinkle it with water mixed with sandalwood and uśīra.
When the poison has spread, one should venesect; this is the supreme treatment. For while the blood is being drawn out, the entire poison is indeed removed. (3.21)
If one is unable to perform venesection, one should extract the blood by means of horns and other such instruments;
first, however, one should administer medicine for the protection of the vital breath.
One should cause [the patient] to drink cow-dung essence with ghee in the full dose;
[this is the protection of the heart]. One should drink ghee, or ghee mixed with honey, or an anti-poisonous medicine (agada) saturated with ghee. (3.23)
In the case of its affliction of the heart-covering, phlegm accumulates in the heart; then, one should cause him to vomit that which has produced heaviness, nausea, and salivation. (3.24)
With liquids excluding sour gruel, horse-gram, oil, wine, and the like— [as for emetic drugs]—
the pulp from the fruit of the *ikṣvāku* mixed with whey; 3.25.
One should administer it for the purpose of emesis, as it is supremely beneficial for one afflicted by poison;
or, one should drink well-cooked buttermilk with honey and rock salt.
Having placed equal parts of *viśvaduḥsparśa*, black pepper, and the force of poison in the mouth, one should repeatedly apply it to the ears and the head of the person who has been bitten.
They should slowly perform fifty simultaneous breath-expulsions;
this supreme method destroys the poison located in the three elements beginning with the skin. (3.28)

Having well-ground the root, flower, leaf, and [other parts] of the excellent *kanyā* plant, it should be drunk with milk or water in all cases of poisoning; this is the universal remedy for all poisons.
This preparation of ointments and so forth is the foremost. || 3.29 ||
By drinking it, by the method of external application, by nasal drops, or by water mixed with powdered ṭaṅkaṇa,
every kind of poison is destroyed in an instant.
Just as the rays of the young sun [dispel] the darkness of night. || 3.30 ||
Having ground together *taṇḍulīya*, *aśvagandhā*, and soot from a cowshed with water, one may eliminate poison by means of drinking it or applying it as an ointment. (3.31)

One should repeatedly cover the mouth of the bitten person with a hand smeared with the leaves of *arka* that have been digested by *hiṅgu*. This, when observed, results in the swift emergence of health.
Poison produced by snakes and other such creatures is quickly destroyed. || 3.32 ||
A piece of cloth, well-impregnated with the thoroughly ripened decoction of *kataka* seeds,
having been dried in the rays of the sun, when placed upon sesame oil...
And having thoroughly examined it, one should not embark upon a boat. || 3.33 ||
Having ground salt or asafoetida together with the leaf of the *dinakṛt* (sun-maker) tree and human urine, an ointment [applied] destroys all poisons without exception. (3.34)
Having ground the leaf of the *naktamāla* together with buffalo dung, one should apply it to the bite and bind it; this is an excellent remedy for removing poison and swelling. (3.35)
In the case of a snakebite, one should perform an irrigation with cold water mixed with sandalwood paste;
this quickly destroys swelling, burning, and pain.
Just as the young sun dispels the darkness of night. || 3.36 ||
And on the fifth day of the dark fortnight, the physician, having collected the seeds of the *śigru* tree, should again join them with that which is designated by the fourth, the sixth, and the moon.
Having thoroughly ground the root of *ketakī* and formed it into pills, one should powder *ṭaṅkaṇa*, mix it therein, and dry it completely. (3.38)
In cases of urinary obstruction for those afflicted by poison, this should be administered with lukewarm water;
this supreme [remedy] is kept secret in the scriptures by physicians of great wisdom. (3.39)
Having ground the roots of *trimūrti*, *nimba*, *nīlī*, and *karañja* with water from their leaves,
one immediately destroys all poison by means of drinking and other such applications. (3.40)
[The pills:
Having ground together kośātakī, vacā, hiṅgu, śirīṣa, and vyoṣa with the milk of *arka* or alternatively with goat’s urine, [one should form pills]. 3.41.
One should administer a drink and nasal drops made from the juice of *śigru* bark with *droṇa* water,
and one should prepare an ointment (*añjana*) from the juice of betel leaves.
[The Small Aśvagandhā Pill]: Aśvagandhā, vacā, śirīṣa, and the three pungents (kaṭutraya) should be infused with the juice of plantain (rambhā).
Through the application of such and such actions, such as drinking [medicines] and so forth, even one bitten by Takṣaka rises up. (3.43)
Having ground together the two types of *kaṇā* poison, rock salt (*saindhava*), and *ṭaṅkaṇa*, along with asafoetida (*hiṅgu*) and yellow orpiment (*haritāla*),
one should form them into pills using "thunderbolt-water" (*vajrāmbu*).
One should perform the drinking of water and other rites with the water of Vaikuṇṭha.
[The *Mṛtasaṃjīvanī*]: Śirīṣa seed, *viṣa*, *śariva*,
and *vacā* enriched with juice and combined with yellow orpiment.
Combined with devadālī, bakula seeds, asafoetida, realgar, the three pungents (vyoṣa), and onion. || 3.45 ||
Having made a pill ground with vajra-water and dried in the shade, one should indeed drink it with lukewarm water; all [applications], including ointments, are to be used with human urine.
And one should perform nasal medication with the water of Vaikuṇṭha.
An ointment for the head with that same [substance], and likewise an eye-salve with breast milk—
this pill, known as *Mṛtasaṃjīvanī*, is a destroyer of poison.
Just as the herb Mṛtasaṃjīvanī, which once pierced Śakrajit’s power and bestowed happiness upon the son of Sumitrā, likewise brings happiness to men. (3.48)
[The *Hiṅgvādi-guṭikā*]:

Having ground equal parts of asafoetida, the three pungents (*vyoṣa*), *aśvagandhā*, buffalo dung, cow dung, and rock salt with the milks of the sun-plant (*arka*) and the moon-plant (*indu*), one should again form pills and saturate them seven times.

If the bitten person conquers the mass of poison by means of drinks and the like, or vomits it up, he reaches the house of death most swiftly even if protected by this Śambhu immediately upon its being drunk. (3.49)
One should place the large pill of *aśvagandhā* and other ingredients inside the hollow of a *naktamāla* tree, and then [place] the *turaṃgamagandhā*.
And having completely covered that face with a certain piece of wood, || 3.50 ||
Having purified it again by placing it for a month right there once more in the hollow of a neem tree, just as before;
And even in a hollow of a *kadamba* tree. || 3.51 ||
Or else, having placed it in the hollow of a long-stalked tree and purified it as before,
[one should take] that which is accompanied by *taṇḍulīyaka* and the two types of *niśā*.
Combined with Vatsanābha, Dhavala, and Arka.
One should grind it with the juice of *nīlikā* leaves, mixed with iron-copper dust,
for three, two, or even one day.
And for five days, [one should bathe] in sandalwood water. || 3.53 ||
One should grind it for three days in water extracted from a *nāgara* plant, and a pill should be prepared;
this very [remedy] is effective against all the poisons of serpents.
And one should also employ the poisons of the *ghoṇasa* and other such snakes. || 3.54 ||
This [remedy] alone is sufficient through its power everywhere against the disease of poison; what need is there for other medicines devised for those afflicted by poison? (3.55)
[The linctus that removes poison:
Having thoroughly ground the seeds of the *mṛdaṅgaphalikā* with the fresh juice of the *nāgavīrudh*, the wise man should then place it in a bronze vessel. 3.56.
Then, having drawn out pure water from it into an auspicious vessel,
the best of physicians should add an equal portion of nimba oil.
One should grind sulphur into powder and add it in a fifth part;
one should likewise add an equal amount of mercury (śivabīja), purified by the juice of betel leaf. (3.58)
One should rub everything with the hand, unifying it according to the rule, until this becomes waterless; this is the elixir that destroys poison.
Having thoroughly ground black pepper, the fruit of white guñjā, and the seed of bakula in the juice of jambīra, one should [administer it] when the poison has been neutralized.
Let him apply an ointment to both eyes for protection against all poisons:
namely, asafoetida, black pepper, guñjā seeds, and the stone of the bakula fruit, mixed with mercury.
Having ground together in the waters of Vaikuṇṭha the seeds of bitter gourd, the semen of Śiva, and sulphur, one obtains a nasal medicine that destroys poison. (3.62)
Having ground [the herbs] for three days with the juice of *śirīṣa* leaves and added the juice of bitter gourd (*kaṭutumbī*),
one should cook clarified butter with those medicinal pastes.
By applying that as an ointment, one may destroy poison located in the wounds caused by teeth, such as those of a ladle or similar objects.
[Treatment for immobilized poison:
A decoction prepared with *upakuñjikā*, combined with milk, [should be administered]. (3.64)
Having drunk poison, one may overcome its rigidity through unwholesome conduct and other such means;
[this is achieved by] a preparation made from the heartwood, root-bark, leaves, flowers, and fruits of the *śirīṣa* tree. (3.65)
A decoction drunk with clarified butter quickly destroys even long-standing poison, whether it be dissolved in the tissues or administered with milk, or else prepared as a decoction. (3.66)
Indeed, a decoction (kvātha) prepared with garlic and ginger is highly beneficial in that case;
for one bitten by [a snake], one should apply a stream of cold water upon the head. 3.67.
One should apply [the oil] smeared with ghee until a state of extreme coolness is reached;
thereafter, for the sake of pacifying numbness, one should use black pepper with lukewarm water. (3.68)
Water is the supreme medicine for the elimination of that poison; once the poison has subsided, one should subsequently treat the aggravated disorder that has become even more intense. (3.69)
When pacifying and purifying treatments have been duly administered with the prescribed medicines,
one should prepare ghee processed with the juice of *nīlī* leaves and the paste made from their roots.
[May there be auspiciousness!
One should employ this for the purpose of soothing those afflicted by poison, as it is supremely beneficial;
or rather, he who brings extreme happiness to those worlds tormented by poison with the sounds of lutes produced from his wings.

I salute that king of birds who sports upon the banner of the enemy of the Daityas, who is mounted by Hari, adorned with shimmering golden wings, with the king of serpents gliding over his white throat, and who fulfills the desires of those who bow before him by bestowing a multitude of cherished fruits. (3.71)
Whatever I have spoken incorrectly, whether through ignorance or by mistake, the virtuous, having examined it all correctly, ought to forgive me. (3.72)
May there be auspiciousness.
